newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French Suez, Lyonnaise lift veil on talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French Suez, Lyonnaise lift veil on talks.

text.p: French conglomerates Lyonnaise des Eaux-Dumez and Cie de Suez lifted a lengthy veil of silence Friday to confirm they were in merger talks.
The companies ended over a week of frenzied stock market and media speculation on an alliance with a brief statement that their boards would consider a merger plan on April 11.

The joint statement said the Suez and Lyonnaise boards would meet on April 1 and April 2, respectively, to approve 1996 results, and would hold special meetings April 11 "to discuss a merger plan between the two companies."
Spokesmen at both companies declined all further comment.
However, one source close to the deal said a straight merger -- rather than a share swap -- would speed up tying the knot.
"With a share swap, we have to submit a bid, and then wait for the investors to turn in their shares. Then we have to make a minority buy-out bid. That takes time," the source said.
"With a merger, investors have no choice but to turn in their shares. If they don't agree with the merger, they can sell off their new shares afterwards," the source told Reuters.

Analysts say it makes sense to merge the two -- Lyonnaise with its sprawling empire in water distribution, electricity and construction, and Suez, a conglomerate seeking a raison d'etre after selling off investment bank Indosuez and other key assets.
A merger would solve an identity crisis for cash-rich Suez and could provide Lyonnaise with the resources to keep up with expanding rival Cie Generale des Eaux, according to analysts.

A potential political obstacle to an alliance appeared to recede Friday when Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said he had an offer of guarantees from Suez that a deal would not hurt the independence of Belgian utility holding Tractebel.

Tractebel is 65 percent-controlled by Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB). But because SGB itself is controlled by Suez, there were worries in Belgium that a merger between Lyonnaise and Suez could compromise Tractebel's position in the Belgian gas and electricity market.

"There is an approach and willingness on both sides to meet the problems raised by the (Belgian) government," Dehaene told a news conference after the weekly Belgian cabinet meeting. "I am convinced these (talks) will end with an agreement."

Together, Lyonnaise and Suez would jump the French company league, probably to around 10th position in terms of market capitalisation but still behind rival utilities-to-media giant Generale des Eaux.

The firms affected by any deal through their shareholdings or involvement in the sector include a number of major players such as Generale des Eaux, which has an indirect stake in Suez through a 20 percent holding in Belgium's Electrafina.
Generale des Eaux has denied reports that it would try to block a Lyonnaise-Suez alliance by launching a counter-bid for Suez.

Suez, which has sold off assets and has been shoring up its accounts after heavy losses when the property market collapsed in the early 1990s, posted a net attributable loss of 3.96 billion francs in 1995. Lyonnaise profits in the same year fell to 906 million francs from 1.06 billion in 1994.
